What is a probe-drift alarm supposed to signal?

It is intended to signal that evidence from probes has changed in a way relevant to trusting attribution under the shifted condition. Such a signal could prompt caution about knockoff-based credit. The activity does not define a drift statistic, an alarm threshold, or a rule for interpreting every alarm, so we should not describe a specific detection mechanism as already established.
Why use DelayVault Benchmark v1 in calibration?

It supplies a named reference containing learning curves, inert-toggle attribution labels, and interactions-to-80%-oracle-return comparisons with recurrent PPO. It is a reference for the attribution problem the calibration is meant to address: 24% inert-toggle misattribution under the shifted condition previously examined. It is not a prediction of the gated-credit trials’ rate. The activity does not say how that reference is used numerically to set an alarm or what rate the rerun will produce.
Could we just choose an alarm setting that makes the 24% figure disappear?

Not as an evidential claim. Calibrating an alarm against a known failure and measuring attribution in a new run are different things. The 24% reference may inform calibration, but only the 20-seed shifted trials can supply a measured misattribution outcome for the gated-credit setup. The activity does not specify a calibration procedure that guarantees any particular rate.
Is a probe-drift alarm the same thing as proving that conditional-history knockoff exchangeability has failed?

No. An alarm is a proposed warning based on probe evidence. A claim about conditional-history knockoff exchangeability requires its own definition and justification. An alarm firing would not, by itself, prove why a comparison is unreliable; an alarm not firing would not prove that the knockoffs remain valid.
Could the hidden-state mixtures shift while the observed histories remain identical?

Yes—that is the challenge being examined in the shifted DelayVault setting. Recorded histories can look the same while the hidden circumstances associated with them differ. Probe drift may be informative in that situation, but the activity does not establish that the proposed alarms detect every such shift.
What does ‘gated credit’ mean in the rerun?

It means the shifted trials use a condition in which knockoff-based causal credit is subject to a gate rather than being accepted without qualification. The activity does not give the gate’s rule, say whether an alarm directly opens or closes it, or specify what happens to each action without audit support. Those details cannot be inferred from the trial description.
Does the gate turn a knockoff association into an identified action effect?

No. A knockoff-based comparison and an identified intervention contrast are different kinds of evidence. Gating can constrain when a signal influences credit, but it cannot by itself provide the unobserved return under an alternative action. A randomized audit can support the comparisons it actually covers; the gate does not enlarge that coverage automatically.
If the gate withholds credit from inert toggles, does that mean it correctly credits every consequential action?

No. Misattribution among inert toggles tests false credit for that assessed class of actions. It does not measure every missed contribution among actions that really affect return. The rerun’s attribution result should be described with its actual assessed actions and decision rule.
What exactly should the 20-seed trials measure for attribution?

They should measure misattribution in the shifted gated-credit condition: how often actions assessed as return-inert receive causal credit under the evaluation’s attribution rule. The activity names the outcome but does not specify the full denominator or the rule that converts an estimate or label into a misattribution event. A reported rate would need that context.
Would any nonzero contrast estimate for an inert toggle count as misattribution?

Only if that is the stated decision rule. A numerical estimate may differ from zero without being used as established causal credit. To compare the shifted gated-credit result with the 24% shift-failure reference, the meaning of a misattribution event needs to remain clear and comparable; the activity does not supply the operational rule.
And what should we measure for savings?

Measure how many environment interactions the gated-credit approach needs to reach the specified return level, then express savings relative to an appropriately defined recurrent PPO reference. DelayVault Benchmark v1 includes interactions-to-80%-oracle-return comparisons, so the return threshold and reference count need to be kept explicit if its metric is used. The activity supplies no new interaction counts or calculated savings.
Could we compare a gated-credit run under the shift with an unshifted recurrent PPO count without saying so?

That would leave the savings percentage ambiguous. A comparison against a benchmark count and one against recurrent PPO evaluated under the shift have different interpretations. The activity names DelayVault Benchmark v1 as a calibration reference, but does not specify which recurrent PPO count is used to calculate savings in the shifted rerun. The eventual report should identify that reference rather than silently treating the two as interchangeable.
Do the probes and audits count toward the gated-credit method’s environment interactions?

Yes, if they involve actions taken in the environment. Those actions are part of the interaction cost of obtaining the evidence used by the method. The activity does not specify a probe or audit budget, so it does not support a numerical cost breakdown.
Does ‘20-seed’ tell us that the rerun has 20 paired recurrent PPO runs?

It specifies 20 seeds for the shifted gated-credit trials. It does not state a pairing procedure or whether recurrent PPO is rerun under those same seeds. Neither a paired analysis nor an uncertainty interval should be asserted from the seed count alone.
Can the alarm be calibrated and evaluated on exactly the same shifted observations without qualification?

That would require care in interpreting an alarm’s apparent performance. The stated activity uses Benchmark v1 and the 24% shift failure for calibration, then calls for a 20-seed shifted rerun. It does not describe how calibration observations are separated from trial observations. We should state that distinction when known, rather than assuming an independent alarm test or claiming one has been completed.
If misattribution is lower in the rerun, can we say the alarm caused the reduction?

Not from that measurement alone. The rerun uses gated credit as well as calibrated alarms, and a change in the measured rate would not isolate either component’s contribution. The activity does not specify a comparison designed to attribute an outcome separately to the alarm or the gate.
What if savings improve but misattribution does not?

That would be a possible difference between the two measured outcomes, not a contradiction in the measurements. Interaction savings assess learning efficiency; misattribution assesses false causal credit. The activity calls for reporting both so that a favorable result on one cannot stand in for a favorable result on the other. No such result is reported yet.
Does the activity tell us whether Γ≤2 bounds cover oracle effects in the shifted rerun?

No. It calls for calibrating probe-drift alarms and measuring misattribution and savings in the 20-seed shifted gated-credit trials. DelayVault Benchmark v1 is the named calibration reference, but no new Γ≤2 bound-coverage measurement is specified for this activity.
What is the narrowest accurate description of the work before we see its measurements?

‘Calibrate probe-drift alarms using DelayVault Benchmark v1 and the 24% shift-failure reference, then conduct 20-seed shifted DelayVault trials with gated knockoff credit and measure misattribution and environment-interaction savings.’ That states the references, trial condition, and outcomes without claiming the alarms work or that the rerun meets an efficiency or attribution target.
What does DelayVault Benchmark v2 contain?

DelayVault Benchmark v2 extends v1 with probe-drift alarms, learning curves for the shifted-mixture gated-credit condition, inert-toggle misattribution, and environment-interaction comparisons with recurrent PPO. That describes the artifact’s contents. It does not state whether the alarms worked, what the learning curves show, or the numerical attribution and interaction results.
What does ‘extends v1’ mean here?

It identifies v1 as the benchmark being extended and names the material added in v2. It does not, by itself, say that v1’s measurements were incorrect or that v2 should be treated as having a particular outcome. The stated addition is the alarm and shifted-mixture gated-credit evaluation material.
Are probe-drift alarms themselves evidence that a hidden-state shift was detected?

Their inclusion means the artifact contains probe-drift alarms. It does not tell us whether an alarm fired, how accurately it detected a shift, or what its signal means in any particular case. Those conclusions would require the alarm definitions and their recorded behavior.
Does ‘probe-drift’ specify an alarm statistic or threshold?
No. It names the kind of alarm, not its calculation or trigger threshold. We should not infer a particular probe comparison, numerical cutoff, or detection rule from the artifact description.
If an alarm fires, does that prove conditional-history knockoff exchangeability has failed?

Not solely from the fact that it is an alarm. Probe drift might flag a reason to scrutinize a knockoff comparison, but a conclusion about conditional-history exchangeability would need the property and the alarm’s relationship to it established. Benchmark v2’s contents list does not provide that validation.
And if no alarm fires, can we trust every knockoff-based attribution?

No. An absent warning would not automatically certify every action comparison. The artifact description provides no guarantee about which hidden-state changes an alarm can detect, and an alarm is not itself an intervention identifying an action’s return effect.
What does ‘shifted-mixture gated-credit learning curves’ tell us?

It tells us that v2 contains learning curves for a condition involving shifted hidden-state mixtures and gated credit. Such curves can show return as learning proceeds with environment interaction. The description gives no plotted values, curve shapes, threshold crossings, or performance conclusion.
Are those curves a comparison between gated credit and ungated credit?

That particular comparison is not specified. The curves are described as belonging to the shifted-mixture gated-credit condition. The artifact also includes recurrent-PPO interaction comparisons, but it does not state that there is an ungated-credit condition or an ablation isolating the gate.
Can we tell from the curves whether the gate prevented false causal credit?

Not from learning curves alone. They concern learning behavior; inert-toggle misattribution is the separate attribution measurement in v2. Even if a curve were favorable, it would not establish that the method correctly distinguished a reward-correlated inert action from one that changes return.
What does it mean for credit to be gated in this artifact?

It identifies the evaluated condition as using gated credit. The artifact description does not specify the gate’s rule, how probe-drift alarms interact with it, or how much credit it allows for any action. We should not infer that every unaudited action receives zero credit or that an alarm automatically shuts off updates.
Does the shifted mixture mean the observed histories must be different?

No such change is required by the phrase. A shift in hidden-state mixtures can matter even when observed histories do not disclose the changed hidden circumstances. V2 names a shifted-mixture condition but does not provide its mixture proportions or a full description of what the agent observes.
Can the learning curves tell us whether a change in the hidden mixture caused any particular outcome?

The curves can provide measurements under the stated condition once examined, but the contents list does not give those measurements or an analysis isolating causes. What is the inert-toggle misattribution item measuring?

V2’s description does not give the rate, underlying counts, or labeling rule.
Does every inert toggle appearing before a reward count as misattributed?

No. Appearing before a reward is an observation; misattribution requires an attribution decision that credits the toggle with an effect it does not have under the relevant counterfactual comparison. The description does not say what decision rule v2 uses to count such an error.
Could I infer a misattribution percentage because v2 includes that measurement?

Does the misattribution item cover all reward-correlated actions?

What are the recurrent-PPO interaction comparisons for?

They provide a learning-efficiency comparison with recurrent PPO as the reference. To interpret savings, the interaction counts need to refer to a common return level and include environment actions used to gather probe or audit evidence. Does v2 already show at least 30% fewer environment interactions?

Should the actions used for probe-drift calibration or randomized audits be included in the interaction count?

If those actions are executed in the environment as part of the evaluated approach, they are environment interactions and belong in its count. The artifact description does not provide a cost breakdown or say how alarm calibration is accounted for, so it cannot support a numerical adjustment.
Is the interaction comparison the same as the inert-toggle misattribution comparison?

Does v2 include a new Γ≤2 bound-coverage result?

A new Γ≤2 coverage measurement is not among the additions explicitly named for v2. Could we treat the probe-drift alarms as identifying unaudited action effects?

No. An alarm concerns possible drift in evidence used for attribution. Identification of a counterfactual action contrast requires support for the specified action intervention under the relevant conditions; an alarm does not supply outcomes for untested alternative actions. Its role should remain distinct from randomized-audit evidence and from sensitivity bounds.
Does the ‘v2’ name imply the safeguards are ready for deployment?

No. A versioned benchmark artifact records material for assessment. Its name and contents do not state that the alarms or gated credit have passed a particular test, or that a deployment decision has been made.
Can we say how many seeds the v2 material uses?

The v2 contents description does not itself state a seed count. Its extension of v1 should not be used to assign an unstated count to every new curve or comparison. A report of v2’s numerical results should specify the repetitions applicable to each measurement.
What would I need to inspect before claiming the alarm-and-gate setup worked under the shift?

You would need the alarms’ recorded behavior and interpretation, the shifted-mixture learning measurements, the inert-toggle misattribution result, and the recurrent-PPO interaction comparison at a clearly matched return. You would also need to keep an observed outcome for the combined setup distinct from a claim that either the alarm or gate individually caused it. V2’s description identifies material to inspect but supplies none of those conclusions.
Can you give me a concise description of the artifact that stays within what is stated?

‘DelayVault Benchmark v2 extends v1 with probe-drift alarms, shifted-mixture gated-credit learning curves, inert-toggle misattribution measurements, and environment-interaction comparisons with recurrent PPO.’ That reports its contents without assigning results to the alarms, attribution measurement, or interaction comparison.

I want to develop SentinelCredit: randomized probes identify action contrasts, while shift-robust sensitivity bounds suppress unsupported credit for distractors and gate recurrent-PPO advantages. Can we unpack the proposal?

SentinelCredit proposes a division of labor. Randomized probes provide intervention evidence for the action contrasts they cover. Shift-robust sensitivity bounds limit what can be claimed when attribution depends on less direct evidence, particularly for actions correlated with delayed rewards but not responsible for them. Those limits would govern which attribution-related advantages influence recurrent PPO training. This is a proposed approach, not a finding that its bounds work or that its training is more efficient.
What do you mean by an action contrast here?

It is a counterfactual comparison of subsequent expected return under one action versus a specified alternative at a decision point. The observed history, the alternative action, and how later decisions are handled all affect the meaning of that comparison. An action’s mere association with a later reward is not itself the contrast.
Is ‘contribution’ an absolute property of an action?

Not without a specified comparison. An action might change expected return relative to one alternative but not another, and its effect can depend on the observed history. SentinelCredit’s intended attributions therefore need to stay tied to defined action contrasts rather than an unqualified assertion that an action deserves a fixed amount of credit everywhere.
Does a randomized probe reveal what would have happened under both actions in one trajectory?

No. Each trajectory follows the action actually assigned. Randomizing between eligible alternatives can support a comparison of expected returns across assignments, but it does not disclose the missing counterfactual outcome for an individual occurrence. ‘Identify’ applies to a defined, covered contrast under appropriate conditions, not to both potential outcomes for every trajectory.
Which conditions matter for a probe-based identification claim?

The random assignment must be valid for the specified action comparison, and the compared alternatives must have support where the contrast is defined. Subsequent return and the continuation after the probed action also need consistent definitions. The proposal does not specify a probe schedule or establish that every action-history pair meets those conditions.
If the agent sees only part of the environment, can randomization still help?

Yes. Hidden circumstances may affect return, but a valid randomized assignment can keep those circumstances from determining which probed alternative is chosen in the covered comparison. The resulting contrast is still conditional on the observed setting used to define it; randomization does not reveal the hidden state or automatically identify an effect at an unprobed history.
How do delayed rewards enter the comparison?

The return being contrasted can include rewards arriving after further observations and decisions. A probed action may change that downstream course, and those consequences can belong to its return contrast if the same continuation rule is specified for both alternatives. A later reward on the realized path alone does not tell us which earlier action caused it.
Could the probe identify the effect of every intervening action before that reward?

No. It supports the contrast for the action choice that was randomized, under the specified continuation. Later actions can be part of the causal pathway following that choice, but assigning each later action its own contribution requires its own counterfactual question and adequate evidence.
What counts as a distractor for SentinelCredit?

In this proposal, the concern is an action that appears predictive of delayed reward without having a supported effect on the relevant return contrast. An action might accompany favorable circumstances yet be causally irrelevant to return. The proposal aims to suppress unsupported causal credit for such actions; it does not supply a particular distractor set or a numerical classification rule.
Would SentinelCredit automatically call any action without a probe a distractor?

No. Lack of direct probe coverage means the probe does not identify that contrast; it does not establish that the action has zero effect. ‘Unsupported credit’ describes a claim that exceeds the available causal evidence, not proof that the action being considered is inert.
Where do shift-robust sensitivity bounds fit?

They are proposed to express limits on action contributions when hidden confounding and shifts make an observational attribution uncertain. Instead of treating a correlation as an exact effect, a bound would describe the contribution values still possible under its explicit assumptions. ‘Shift-robust’ states the intended resilience to relevant changes in circumstances; the proposal does not specify a class of shifts, a bound formula, or demonstrated robustness.
Does shift-robust mean that all hidden-state shifts are covered?

No. A meaningful robustness claim must define which shifts the bounds allow and which information and assumptions support the bounds under those shifts. The name alone cannot guarantee coverage under arbitrary changes in hidden circumstances. SentinelCredit proposes shift-robust bounds, leaving their precise scope to be established.
Why might conditioning on observed history be insufficient under a shift?

Identical recorded histories can correspond to different hidden circumstances. If the mix of those circumstances changes, the relationship between observed action choices and delayed return can also change without an obvious difference in the recorded history. A sensitivity bound intended to be shift-robust needs to account for the shifts it claims to tolerate; matching on history alone does not settle that question.
Are these bounds the same as confidence intervals around an interaction-saving estimate?

No. A hidden-confounding sensitivity bound limits possible counterfactual action contrasts under specified allowances. A confidence interval for interaction savings would concern uncertainty about learning efficiency. They address different quantities and should not be substituted for one another.
Does SentinelCredit specify a value for a sensitivity parameter such as Γ?

No. It proposes shift-robust sensitivity bounds but gives neither a numerical parameter range nor a mathematical sensitivity model. We should not assign the bounds a particular Γ value or numerical width as though one had been chosen.
If a bound contains zero, should the action receive no credit?

Containing zero means the bound does not rule out a zero return contribution under its assumptions. That limits a claim of established nonzero causal responsibility, but the proposal does not specify an exact rule mapping such a bound to zero advantage or to any other update. ‘Gate’ and ‘suppress unsupported credit’ indicate the intended caution, not a fully defined weighting function.
What if a bound excludes zero?

Zero exclusion could support a nonzero contribution within the stated shift and hidden-confounding allowances, provided the bound applies to that precise contrast. It would not establish an effect under unrestricted shifts or reveal the exact counterfactual return. The proposal does not promise that any particular bound will exclude zero.
Can the bound create information for an action alternative that never occurs?

Not simply by being called a sensitivity bound. If a comparison lacks randomized coverage and lacks relevant observational support, an informative bound would require additional explicit restrictions. SentinelCredit should distinguish what the probes identify, what its assumptions can bound, and what remains unresolved.
How would the bounds suppress distractor credit without claiming to prove every distractor is inert?

They could constrain whether the available evidence warrants treating an observed action–reward association as a causal contribution. Suppressing unsupported credit means not promoting that association into a strong policy-training signal when the bounded contrast remains uncertain. It is different from proving a zero effect: an uncertain action may matter, but the evidence may not justify crediting it as if its effect were known.
What exactly is being gated in recurrent PPO?

The proposal says the sensitivity bounds gate advantages used to train recurrent PPO. Conceptually, attribution-related advantage information would be admitted or constrained according to what the action-contrast evidence supports. It does not specify a numerical gate, a new PPO architecture, or a rule for each type of action comparison.
Does gating mean all advantages come only from randomized probes?

That is not stated. Probes identify covered contrasts; bounds are intended to govern credit where other evidence is less decisive. The proposal does not say every nonprobed advantage must be removed, nor does it license treating every observational advantage as causally identified.
Could a strict gate overlook actions that really affect return?

That is a possible concern, not a reported outcome. Limiting unwarranted credit could also limit use of uncertain but informative contributions. Whether SentinelCredit can avoid false distractor credit while still learning effectively is an empirical question; the proposal does not guarantee the balance.
Is SentinelCredit a replacement for recurrent PPO?

Not as described. It proposes to gate the advantages that train recurrent PPO. SentinelCredit names the proposed combination of randomized action probes, shift-robust sensitivity bounds, and gated credit, rather than a specified replacement for recurrent PPO.
Would the randomized probes count when measuring environment-interaction efficiency?

Yes. If a probe takes an action in the environment, that action is an environment interaction. Any comparison of interactions to matched return would need to count probe interactions on SentinelCredit’s side. The proposal supplies no probe budget or measured interaction count.
Can we say SentinelCredit already reaches matched returns using 30% fewer environment interactions than recurrent PPO?

No. That is the broader delayed-reward learning target, not an outcome reported for SentinelCredit. The proposal describes how it intends to make action credit more causally defensible and use that credit in recurrent PPO training; it gives no matched-return benchmark or savings percentage.
Does improving the policy establish that the causal attribution is correct?

No. An action can predict reward and still have no counterfactual effect on return. Learning efficiency and causal identification need separate support. SentinelCredit’s probe-based identification claims must stay within probe coverage, and the interpretation of its bounds must stay within their stated hidden-confounding and shift assumptions.
What is the most faithful one-sentence description of the proposal?

‘Develop SentinelCredit using randomized probes to identify covered action-return contrasts and shift-robust sensitivity bounds to suppress unsupported credit for correlated distractors and gate the advantages used to train recurrent PPO.’ That preserves the roles of the components without asserting universal identification, shift immunity, or a measured efficiency gain.
Can SentinelCredit keep inert-toggle misattribution below 10% under hidden-state shifts while preserving 30% environment-interaction savings?

That is an open, joint question. One part asks whether SentinelCredit avoids falsely crediting inert toggles when hidden circumstances change; the other asks whether it can do so while reaching matched returns with 30% fewer environment interactions than recurrent PPO. Its proposed probes and shift-robust bounds provide a way to investigate both, but the proposal does not establish either outcome.
Why treat those as two separate outcomes if we want both at once?

Because they measure different properties. Inert-toggle misattribution concerns whether an action with no relevant effect on return is assigned causal credit. Interaction savings concern how much environment experience is needed to reach a matched return. The question requires both to hold under the shifted setting; success on either measure alone cannot answer it.
What would count as misattributing an inert toggle?

It would mean assigning a toggle causal responsibility for return despite its relevant action intervention having no effect on return. Merely observing it before a delayed reward, or finding it predictive of that reward, is not itself an attribution. A measured rate would need an explicit rule for what SentinelCredit output counts as assigning credit and which assessed toggles form the denominator.
Does a nonzero estimated contrast automatically count as false attribution?

Not necessarily. An estimate can differ numerically from zero without being treated as established causal credit, particularly when its uncertainty is acknowledged. Whether an estimate becomes a false attribution depends on the stated decision rule. The question gives a rate threshold, but not that operational rule.
Is ‘below 10%’ inclusive of exactly 10%?

No. ‘Below 10%’ is strict: exactly 10% would not meet that condition. It also refers specifically to misattribution among the assessed inert toggles, not to an error rate for every action contribution.
What does ‘under hidden-state shifts’ add to the attribution requirement?

It asks whether the low false-credit rate persists when the underlying circumstances change in ways that may not be captured by the observed history. An action can retain an apparent association with delayed reward while that association provides unreliable evidence about its intervention effect. The question does not specify a particular shift, its magnitude, or how many shifted conditions are to be examined.
If two observed histories look identical, can their hidden-state mixtures still differ?

Yes. Partial observation permits distinct hidden circumstances to produce the same recorded history. A change in their mixture could alter how useful a history-conditioned observational comparison is, without giving the agent an obvious new observed-history category. That is a general reason to examine shifts; it does not specify the shift used in any SentinelCredit test.
Would the toggle stop being inert if the hidden-state mixture changes?

Not merely because the mixture changes. For a misattribution test, the toggles must be assessed against their relevant intervention effects in the shifted setting. If those effects remain zero, causal credit remains false credit. If an effect changes, the target comparison must be described accordingly rather than assuming that an action is inert in every possible circumstance.
How might SentinelCredit’s randomized probes help with that question?

A valid probe can support a counterfactual return contrast for the actions and observed-history settings it actually randomizes. That gives a basis for distinguishing a return-changing choice from one that only accompanies reward. Under a shift, however, the probe result still has the scope of its actual assignment and coverage; it cannot establish the effect of every unaudited toggle or every unexamined hidden circumstance.
Could randomized probes alone guarantee a false-attribution rate below 10%?

No. Their existence does not guarantee coverage of every relevant toggle comparison, precise estimates, or correct decisions about causal credit. The proposed shift-robust sensitivity bounds are intended to constrain claims outside directly supported comparisons, but their presence also does not guarantee a numerical rate. The below-10% condition has to be measured.
What makes a sensitivity bound ‘shift-robust’ rather than simply cautious?

A meaningful shift-robust claim would specify which changes in hidden circumstances are allowed and show that the bound remains applicable under those changes. Calling a bound robust without stating the permitted shifts and assumptions would not establish that property. SentinelCredit proposes such bounds; their precise scope and performance under shifts are not specified by this question.
Does a bound containing zero establish that the toggle is inert?

No. It means a zero contribution remains compatible with the information and assumptions behind that bound; nonzero values may also remain possible. It can limit an unsupported claim of definite causal credit without positively proving a null effect. The reference for a toggle’s inertness is its relevant action intervention, not merely whether a bound includes zero.
What if the bound excludes zero for an inert toggle?

That would warrant scrutiny of the bound’s applicability and the alignment of its contrast with the toggle’s intervention reference. Zero exclusion under a bound is conditional on its assumptions; it is not a guarantee that an action truly affects return. The question does not report such a case or a bound-coverage result.
Would gating recurrent-PPO advantages make false credit impossible?

No. Gating is meant to constrain how attribution evidence enters training, but its effect depends on the rule used and on whether the supporting probes and bounds remain valid under the shift. A gate cannot turn an unsupported action–reward association into an identified effect. Nor does the proposal specify a gate that guarantees zero false attributions.
Could a cautious gate help attribution but cost environment interactions?

It could; that is part of the tension the question asks us to examine. Withholding questionable credit may change learning, while randomized probes carried out in the environment consume interactions. Whether the combined approach keeps false attribution below 10% and still preserves the interaction saving is not determined by the design description alone.

It compares the total environment interactions SentinelCredit and recurrent PPO need to reach the same specified return level. A 30% saving means SentinelCredit uses 70% as many interactions as recurrent PPO for that comparison. The question does not specify a numerical return threshold, a task set, or an observed interaction count.
Should probes be included in SentinelCredit’s total?

Yes. A randomized probe action taken in the environment is an environment interaction. Excluding those actions while using the evidence they provide would overstate SentinelCredit’s savings. The proposed approach does not supply a probe rate or a cost breakdown here.
Could we say savings were preserved if SentinelCredit uses fewer interactions but reaches a lower return?

No SentinelCredit saving is reported in this question. ‘Preserving’ describes the performance condition being sought alongside robustness of attribution; it should not be read as a measured SentinelCredit result. Whether that level of savings holds under hidden-state shifts remains open.

Yes. It might reach the matched return efficiently while continuing to credit reward-correlated actions whose interventions have no effect. The reverse is also possible: it might avoid false toggle credit but require too many interactions. The question asks whether SentinelCredit can satisfy both conditions in the shifted setting.
If the measured toggle rate were under 10%, would that establish that every correlated distractor is handled correctly?

No. It would be a result about the assessed inert toggles under the evaluated hidden-state shifts and the stated attribution rule. No. Misattribution and interaction savings are not bound-coverage measurements. Coverage would separately ask whether oracle effects lie inside the corresponding sensitivity bounds. And could favorable bounds alone establish the 30% saving?

No. Bounds concern what can be said about action contributions under stated assumptions. The 30% condition requires an empirical environment-interaction comparison at matched return against recurrent PPO, counting probes. Attribution evidence and learning efficiency have to be evaluated separately even when they are part of one approach.

It would name the hidden-state shifts examined, define which inert toggles and credit decisions determine the misattribution rate, and state the common return level and recurrent-PPO interaction reference for savings. It would report whether misattribution is strictly below 10% and whether the interaction saving is 30% under that same evaluated SentinelCredit setup, without extrapolating to every possible shift or unaudited action.

Yes. That states the proposal and leaves the joint outcome open. Its mechanisms suggest what to examine, but no SentinelCredit result here establishes the inert-toggle rate or the matched-return interaction saving under hidden-state shifts.

Yes. An action can occur alongside a delayed reward without changing return when intervened on. The attribution error concerns crediting it as a cause, not merely observing the association.
Does 9% mean that the remaining 91% all had estimated contrasts of exactly zero?

No. The rate concerns misattribution decisions, not a list of numerical contrast estimates. The finding does not state the estimates or labels for individual toggles, or the exact rule that classified each decision.
Do we know how many inert toggles were evaluated?
No underlying count is provided with the 9% figure. We cannot infer the number of toggles or mistaken labels from that percentage alone.
Does that rate tell us whether SentinelCredit correctly credited actions that genuinely affect return?
No. It measures false credit among assessed inert toggles. It does not report missed effects among consequential actions or the accuracy of every action contribution.
Now, what does the 94% coverage figure mean?

It means that 94% of the oracle action contrasts checked lay within their corresponding Γ≤2 sensitivity bounds. Coverage asks whether the reference contrast is inside the bound. It is different from asking whether the method credited an inert toggle or how many environment interactions it saved.
Does 94% coverage mean the remaining 6% of checked oracle contrasts were outside the bounds?

For the reported set, yes: if each checked contrast is classified as covered or not covered, the complement of 94% coverage is 6% noncoverage. The result does not identify those contrasts or explain why their bounds did not contain them.
Does it tell us whether the bounds were narrow?

No. A bound can contain its oracle contrast while still spanning a wide range of possible effects. Coverage alone provides no bound widths, endpoints, or measure of how precisely the contrasts were localized.
Could I call 94% the accuracy of SentinelCredit’s action labels?

No. Its denominator is checked oracle contrasts, and its criterion is inclusion within Γ≤2 bounds. The 9% figure addresses inert-toggle misattribution. Relabeling bound coverage as label accuracy would combine two different measures.
Does a bound covering the oracle also mean it excludes zero?

Not necessarily. A bound may contain both zero and the oracle contrast. Conversely, excluding zero does not ensure that it contains the oracle. The finding reports coverage, not a zero-exclusion percentage.
If a bound contains zero and an oracle contrast, what can we say about causal credit?

We can say that the bound covers that oracle contrast while leaving zero among its permitted values. Under that bound, nonzero causal credit is not established merely by the coverage result. The finding does not say how SentinelCredit’s credit gate handled any individual bound.
Does Γ≤2 mean the hidden confounding on EchoMaze-Delay was measured to be at most 2?

No. Γ≤2 identifies the sensitivity range used for the reported bounds. It is not a measurement of the actual hidden confounding. The bounds’ interpretation remains conditional on their sensitivity model and assumptions, which are not detailed in this result.
Would the 94% figure guarantee coverage under every hidden-state shift?

No. It is the measured coverage of checked oracle contrasts on shifted EchoMaze-Delay. It does not establish the same coverage for other shifts, other tasks, or action comparisons not included in the check.
The audit examined probe contrasts against oracle interventions. Can the 94% figure be read as proof that every probe-based contrast was identified?

No. The reported 94% specifically concerns Γ≤2 bound coverage of oracle contrasts. Whether a given action contrast is identified by a randomized probe depends on valid assignment and support for its compared alternatives. An aggregate bound-coverage percentage does not establish those conditions for every contrast.
Are a probe contrast and a Γ≤2 bound the same thing?

No. A probe contrast is a counterfactual action comparison that randomized assignments may identify where they cover both alternatives. A Γ≤2 bound describes a range of possible contrast values under a specified sensitivity allowance. The latter is not automatically a point estimate or proof of identification.
What would we need to know to decide whether a particular oracle contrast was properly matched to its bound?

They would need to refer to the same action alternatives, observed-history condition, subsequent-return definition, and continuation rule. The 94% aggregate tells us the reported coverage outcome, but supplies no contrast-by-contrast matching details.
Could a strong interaction saving itself verify those causal comparisons?

No. Interaction savings concern learning efficiency against recurrent PPO. Even an approach that reaches return efficiently can misattribute some actions or produce bounds that miss some oracle contrasts. The three reported measurements should be interpreted separately.
Does 9% inert-toggle misattribution prove the Γ≤2 bounds covered the toggles’ oracle effects?

No. A false-credit rate concerns attribution decisions for toggles; bound coverage concerns inclusion of oracle contrasts in sensitivity ranges. The result does not report how the set of misattributed toggles overlaps with the set of uncovered oracle contrasts.
Could I say that the Γ≤2 gate, rather than the probes, specifically caused the measured outcomes?
No. These are outcomes for the evaluated SentinelCredit setup. The figures do not isolate the effect of the gate, probes, or alarm thresholds on savings, misattribution, or coverage.
Do we have a confidence interval for the 32% interaction saving?

None is stated with this finding. The audit called for a paired-bootstrap calculation, but the reported result here provides only the 32% saving, not interval endpoints or a confidence level. We should not supply an interval that is not reported.
What about uncertainty intervals for the 9% and 94%?
No uncertainty intervals for those percentages are stated either. The result gives their measured values and scopes, but not their precision or variation across runs.
Can we infer how the frozen alarm thresholds behaved from these three percentages?

No. The figures describe interaction savings, inert-toggle misattribution, and bound coverage. They do not state whether an alarm fired, how often it fired, or whether a particular alarm decision was correct.
Does the result establish exact causal contributions for actions at histories that were never probed?

No. Γ≤2 bounds remain conditional ranges where they apply, and the aggregate coverage result does not give randomized evidence at unprobed histories. Neither the efficiency saving nor the inert-toggle rate supplies an individual counterfactual return for an unprobed action.
How should I describe the finding without generalizing it beyond shifted EchoMaze-Delay?

‘On shifted EchoMaze-Delay, SentinelCredit used 32% fewer environment interactions than recurrent PPO and misattributed 9% of inert toggles; its Γ≤2 bounds covered 94% of checked oracle action contrasts.’ That preserves the three distinct outcomes and their stated task scope.

I’d like to develop LatentBridge: estimate proximal action contrasts using negative-control proxies and randomized probes, then train recurrent PPO on uncertainty-gated advantages. Can we unpack what this proposes?

LatentBridge proposes an attribution-and-training approach for partially observed reinforcement learning with delayed rewards. Negative-control proxies and randomized probes would help estimate counterfactual action contrasts, though they provide different kinds of evidence. Uncertainty-gated advantages would then govern how those estimates influence recurrent PPO training. This is a proposal, not a claim that the contrasts have been identified or that training has improved.
First, what would an action contrast mean in this proposal?

It would compare expected subsequent return under one action with expected subsequent return under a specified alternative, at a specified decision point or observed history. Both sides of the comparison need the same definition of return and a clear rule for subsequent decisions. That makes the contrast a question about changing an action, rather than simply observing that an action tends to precede reward.
Does the word ‘proximal’ mean the reward must arrive soon after the action?

No. Here ‘proximal’ describes the proposed use of proxy-based causal information in the presence of hidden confounding; it should not be read as a requirement for an immediately following reward. The action contrast can concern delayed return. The proposal does not specify a return horizon or a particular proximal estimator.
Why would LatentBridge need proxies if it also uses randomized probes?

They address different evidential situations. A valid randomized probe can inform a contrast for the actions and histories it actually covers. Negative-control proxies are proposed to help reason about hidden factors when an action comparison cannot simply be read from randomized assignments. Having probes somewhere does not supply randomized evidence for every action-history comparison.
What is a negative-control proxy, conceptually?

It is an observed variable used to learn about otherwise hidden sources of bias through a carefully specified causal relationship. Calling it a negative control imposes restrictions on what it can directly affect or how it relates to the action and return being studied. Merely finding an observed variable correlated with return does not make it a valid negative-control proxy; its proposed role and assumptions must be stated.
Are you saying the proxies reveal the hidden state?

No. A proxy can carry information relevant to hidden circumstances without measuring those circumstances exactly. Whether it is sufficient for a particular proximal action contrast depends on assumptions about its relationship to hidden factors, actions, and returns. LatentBridge does not claim that partial observation has been eliminated.
Would any predictive feature make a suitable proxy?

Not automatically. Predicting delayed reward and satisfying the restrictions needed for a negative-control analysis are different things. A feature could be predictive because it directly reflects consequences of the action, for example, making it unsuitable for a proposed negative-control role under some definitions. The proposal has not named particular proxies or established their validity.
What is the hidden-confounding problem the proxies are meant to address?

A hidden factor could influence both the action selected and the later return. If so, a difference in observed returns following two policy-chosen actions may combine an action effect with the hidden factor’s influence. Proxies are proposed as a way to constrain that ambiguity under explicit assumptions, rather than assuming that conditioning on the observed history alone removes it.
Can negative-control proxies by themselves guarantee identification?

No. Proxy-based identification would depend on conditions that make the hidden influence recoverable for the specified contrast, as well as appropriate support for the action comparison. Those conditions must be established or qualified; the label ‘negative control’ is not a proof. If distinct hidden-confounder explanations remain compatible with all the available observations and proxies but imply different interventions, the contrast remains unidentified.
What sorts of conditions would we need to clarify without choosing a specific estimator yet?

At a conceptual level, clarify which variables serve as proxies, what their negative-control restrictions are, how they relate to the hidden factors affecting action selection and return, and what information makes the target contrast recoverable. Proxy informativeness and action support matter alongside those restrictions. That describes questions a proximal analysis would have to answer; it does not assert that LatentBridge already meets them.
Does ‘estimate proximal action contrasts’ promise a point estimate for every history?

No. It states the intended quantity and approach. Some histories may lack the action support, valid proxies, or randomized coverage needed for a reliable estimate, and different assumptions could imply different causal contrasts. The method would need to distinguish supported estimates from comparisons that remain uncertain or unidentifiable.
Where do randomized probes provide a firmer reference?

Where the relevant alternatives are validly randomized with support at the history or defined group being compared, subsequent returns can inform that covered action contrast directly. This can help distinguish a causal effect from an action that merely accompanies favorable circumstances. It does not reveal both possible returns for a single decision, and it does not identify effects outside the probe’s coverage.
Could the probes and proxies be used in the same action comparison?

That is consistent with the proposal, which names both as sources for estimating proximal action contrasts. They should retain their distinct interpretations: randomized assignments support the comparisons they actually cover; a proxy-based inference depends on the validity of its negative-control assumptions. LatentBridge does not specify a formula for combining them or require that every contrast use both.
Would a randomized probe prove that a chosen proxy is a valid negative control?

Not by itself. Probe outcomes can provide intervention evidence for covered action contrasts, but agreement with them would not establish every exclusion or information condition a proxy-based analysis requires. Conversely, a seemingly informative proxy would not extend a probe’s identification claim to actions or histories the probe never varied.
How does delayed reward complicate both sources of evidence?

A reward may arrive after many decisions, making it difficult to tell which preceding actions changed subsequent return and which merely correlated with circumstances favorable to reward. Probe comparisons must use a consistently defined delayed return, and proxy-based contrasts must target that same action intervention rather than just predict the later reward. Neither approach can assign a unique causal contribution to every intermediate action from one rewarded trajectory alone.
If an action is correlated with a delayed reward but has no effect on return, what should the contrast say?

For a comparison in which changing that action truly leaves expected return unchanged, the counterfactual contrast would be zero, even if the action strongly predicts reward in observed trajectories. LatentBridge is proposed to separate those notions. Its components do not guarantee that it will correctly classify every reward-irrelevant action.
Might the effect depend on what the policy does after the action?

Yes. The contrast needs a defined continuation rule. If later decisions respond to observations caused by the initial action, their downstream effects can be part of its return contrast. Fixing later decisions would pose a different question. The proposal does not select a particular continuation rule, so it should be made explicit before interpreting an estimate.
What if two identical observed histories hide different underlying situations?

An effect conditioned on that observed history may average over those hidden situations, and observational action selection may differ between them. Randomization can support its covered comparison despite hidden variation in return, while a proxy analysis needs assumptions sufficient to address hidden selection. Neither the shared observed history nor the presence of a proxy establishes an effect for each individual hidden situation.
Does LatentBridge require every negative-control proxy to have no association with reward?

No. A proxy can be informative precisely because it is associated with hidden circumstances related to return. What makes it a suitable negative control is a specified causal restriction, not the absence of all statistical association. The proposal has not defined those restrictions for any concrete variable.
What does ‘uncertainty-gated advantages’ add after estimating the contrasts?

It proposes using uncertainty about the action contributions to control how attribution-related advantage information enters recurrent PPO training. The aim is to avoid giving an uncertain association the same training authority as a well-supported action contrast. ‘Gated’ does not specify a numerical weight, an all-or-nothing rule, or a particular uncertainty calculation.
Would an action with an uncertain contrast automatically receive zero advantage?

That does not follow from the proposal. Uncertainty gating could constrain the use of an estimate without asserting that the true action effect is zero. The precise mapping from an estimate and its uncertainty to a training advantage remains unspecified.
If a probe supports a contrast, does its advantage bypass the gate?

No bypass rule is stated. Probe-supported contrasts can still be estimated with uncertainty, especially when evidence is limited. The proposal names uncertainty-gated advantages for training; it does not distinguish a class of estimates that must be accepted without qualification.
How would we avoid training recurrent PPO on a proxy that is only predictive?

Keep the proxy’s predictive association separate from its role in a justified causal contrast. Training credit should be interpreted through whatever action-contrast evidence and uncertainty rule LatentBridge ultimately defines, rather than declaring the proxy’s correlation to be an action effect. The proposal has not yet specified the gate or demonstrated that it makes this distinction correctly in practice.
Is LatentBridge meant to replace recurrent PPO?

Not as stated. The proposed uncertainty-gated advantages train recurrent PPO. LatentBridge names the intended contrast-estimation and credit-gating approach, not a specified replacement for recurrent PPO’s policy architecture.
Does adding probes have a cost for an environment-interaction comparison?

Yes. A randomized probe carried out as an action in the environment counts as an environment interaction. If LatentBridge is compared with recurrent PPO on interactions needed to reach matched return, those probe actions belong in LatentBridge’s total. The proposal gives no probe rate, interaction count, or measured savings.
Does the proposal say how many proxies, how many probes, or which delayed-reward tasks to use?

No. It names negative-control proxies, randomized probes, proximal action contrasts, and uncertainty-gated advantages, but gives no proxy set, probe budget, task list, or evaluation result. Those details should not be inserted as if they had already been chosen.
Could good returns establish that the negative controls were valid?

No. A policy could learn efficiently using signals that predict reward even if those signals do not justify a causal attribution. Proxy validity and the identification of action contrasts require their own argument or evidence. Learning performance against recurrent PPO would answer a separate question.
And would a rigorous proximal identification argument establish the learning-efficiency goal?

No. It would establish what can be inferred about specified action interventions under its conditions. Whether training recurrent PPO with uncertainty-gated advantages reaches matched returns with 30% fewer environment interactions than recurrent PPO on delayed-reward tasks would require an interaction-efficiency comparison; this proposal reports none.
What would be the careful way to state the identifiability limit for LatentBridge?

Say that probe-based identification extends only to validly randomized, supported action comparisons, while proxy-based identification depends on stated negative-control and information assumptions. Where neither route resolves hidden confounding, a counterfactual action contrast can remain well defined but not uniquely determined from the available observations. Gating an uncertain estimate does not remove that limit.
Could you give me a compact description that preserves the proposal without implying a completed experiment?

‘Develop LatentBridge to estimate proximal counterfactual action contrasts using negative-control proxies and randomized probes, then use uncertainty-gated advantages to train recurrent PPO.’ Its identification conditions, training rule, and empirical performance remain to be established.
When do negative-control proxies identify unprobed action contrasts under hidden confounding, and can LatentBridge retain at least 30% environment-interaction savings?

Those are two open questions. For an unprobed contrast, identification would require more than a proxy’s correlation with delayed return: the proposed negative controls must satisfy causal restrictions, carry sufficient information about the relevant hidden confounding, and support the specified action comparison. Even if those conditions can be established, whether LatentBridge reaches matched return using ≥30% fewer environment interactions than recurrent PPO is a separate empirical question.
Can we first pin down what an ‘unprobed action contrast’ is?

It is a counterfactual comparison between specified action alternatives at an observed history for which the relevant alternatives were not directly compared by a randomized probe. The target might still be well defined as a difference in expected subsequent return under the two action interventions. ‘Unprobed’ describes a gap in direct randomized evidence, not proof that either action has no effect.
Does the return have to appear right after the action?

No. The contrast can concern delayed return, including consequences that arise after later observations and decisions. To interpret it, both sides need the same return definition and a stated rule for how subsequent decisions are made. A proxy that predicts a later reward does not, merely for that reason, identify which earlier action changed that return.
Why might ordinary comparisons of the two actions be misleading even if we condition on observed history?

Partially observed histories can hide factors that influence both which action is chosen and the later return. Two actions may both occur following the same recorded history, yet be selected under different hidden circumstances. A difference between their observed returns can then combine selection effects with the effect of changing the action.
How can a negative-control proxy help with that if it does not reveal the hidden state?

Its intended role is to provide information about the hidden influence under carefully specified restrictions on its own causal relationships. If those restrictions and the information it carries are sufficient for the chosen proximal contrast, an observational comparison may be corrected or connected to the intervention contrast. That possibility is conditional: a proxy does not have to reveal hidden state exactly, but merely calling a variable a negative control does not establish that it contains enough usable information.
What does ‘negative control’ exclude, conceptually?

It requires specifying a relationship that the candidate proxy does *not* have with the intervention or return, while allowing it to carry information about the hidden circumstances of interest. Exactly which relationship is excluded depends on the proxy’s proposed role. LatentBridge has not named concrete proxy variables or fixed their negative-control restrictions, so we cannot certify any particular candidate from its label alone.
Could I choose any observation that predicts return as the proxy?

No. Predictive association may itself arise through an action’s effects, or through a relationship incompatible with the proposed negative-control restriction. Proxy validity is a causal condition, not a measure of predictive accuracy. The analysis has to explain why the proposed proxy is suitable for identifying the specified action contrast under hidden confounding.
Is a valid negative control enough on its own?

Not necessarily. Its restrictions must be accompanied by sufficient information about the hidden influence to resolve the ambiguity between action selection and return, along with support for the action alternatives being compared. If multiple hidden-confounder explanations still agree on all observed actions, histories, proxies, and returns but imply different intervention effects, the contrast is not identified from that information.
What do you mean by ‘sufficient information’ without committing to a particular proximal estimator?

The proxy observations must distinguish the relevant hidden influences well enough that the proposed relationship between observable quantities and the counterfactual contrast has an unambiguous solution under the stated assumptions. If different hidden influences remain indistinguishable through the proxies yet imply different action effects, proxy information is insufficient. A formal LatentBridge argument would need to state the relevant condition precisely; the question alone does not provide one.
Could many observations of one action compensate for never observing its alternative at that history?

Not without further restrictions. Having data for one action does not directly supply the return under an unsupported alternative. Even informative proxies cannot automatically fill a missing action-comparison arm. Any identification claim for an unprobed contrast needs to explain the action support it uses and where, if anywhere, information is carried between histories.
Suppose both actions do occur in observational trajectories. Does that establish identification?

No. Their occurrence supplies observational overlap, which makes a comparison possible, but does not remove hidden confounding. Proxy-based identification would additionally require its negative-control restrictions and information conditions. Overlap is not a substitute for those assumptions, just as those assumptions should not silently be used to claim support for an action never represented in the relevant comparison.
Would randomized probes settle the matter for an unprobed history by validating the proxy elsewhere?

Not automatically. A probe identifies only the action alternatives and history setting it actually covers under valid assignment and support. Comparing a proxy-based estimate with a probed contrast could be informative about that covered comparison, but agreement there does not prove the proxy restrictions or identify an unprobed contrast at a different history. Extending the result requires its own justification.
Could the probes still be useful to LatentBridge even if they are sparse?

Yes. Where they validly vary both alternatives, they offer direct intervention evidence for the defined contrast and can provide a reference against which other attribution evidence is examined. Their sparsity limits which histories and actions they cover and may leave estimates uncertain. The proposal does not set a probe rate or specify a rule for combining probes with proxies.
Does partial observation mean even a randomized probe cannot identify a contrast?

Not categorically. Valid randomized assignment can identify an expected contrast for a covered observed-history comparison despite hidden circumstances influencing return, provided the required conditions hold. It does not reveal both potential returns for any one trajectory or establish the same effect for each hidden circumstance. Proxy reasoning for an unprobed contrast addresses a different evidential gap.
What if two hidden-confounder models fit every recorded proxy and return equally well?

If they also imply different counterfactual returns under the same action intervention, the observations and proxies do not uniquely determine that contrast. A claimed proximal identification result would need assumptions that exclude this ambiguity. If those assumptions cannot be justified, LatentBridge should describe the remaining uncertainty rather than report an unqualified causal effect.
Does uncertainty-gated training resolve that nonidentification?

No. A gate can limit how much an uncertain action estimate influences recurrent PPO advantages, but cannot turn an unidentified contrast into a known one. Keeping unsupported causal credit out of an update is different from establishing that the action has no effect or knowing exactly how large its effect is.
Is there a risk that suppressing uncertainty also suppresses a genuinely consequential action?

There could be. An action may matter even if the available proxies and probes cannot establish its contribution. A cautious advantage gate might avoid unwarranted credit yet leave useful effects underused. The question asks whether LatentBridge can handle attribution and retain interaction efficiency; neither outcome follows from the proposed gate alone.
How do we distinguish an action that is merely correlated with delayed reward from one with a proximal contribution?

The defining distinction is intervention: would expected subsequent return change if the action were set to the specified alternative, under the stated continuation? An action can predict a delayed reward because of hidden circumstances yet have a zero contrast. Negative-control proxies and randomized probes are proposed as ways to address that distinction, but their validity must be shown for the relevant comparison rather than assumed from predictive performance.
Now the efficiency side: what does retaining ≥30% savings mean?

At a matched return level, LatentBridge would have to need no more than 70% as many environment interactions as recurrent PPO. The ≥30% figure refers to a reduction relative to recurrent PPO’s interaction count, not a 30% increase in return. This question states the target, not an observed LatentBridge saving.
Would probe actions count in those environment interactions?

Yes. Randomized probes executed in the environment consume interactions and belong in LatentBridge’s count. Obtaining attribution information through probes cannot be treated as free when comparing interactions needed to reach matched return. No probe budget or interaction totals have been supplied for LatentBridge.
Could we report a 30% saving if LatentBridge stops after reaching a lower return than recurrent PPO?

No. The return must be matched for the interaction reduction to meet the stated target. Using fewer interactions to reach a lower return, or attaining a higher return at the same interaction count, answers a different question.
Does the question specify which delayed-reward tasks or how many seeds should establish that saving?

No. It asks whether LatentBridge can retain ≥30% interaction savings, but supplies no task list, seed count, matched-return threshold, or aggregation rule. An evaluation would need to state its scope before an across-task or per-task savings claim could be interpreted.
Could success on the efficiency comparison validate the negative-control proxies?

No. A policy can learn from signals correlated with return without those signals identifying the causal contribution of an action. Proxy validity and identification of unprobed contrasts require an independent, appropriately scoped argument. Likewise, identifying an action contrast would not demonstrate the interaction-savings target.
What is the cautious answer to the original two-part question?

Negative-control proxies can identify an unprobed action contrast only under explicit, adequate negative-control restrictions, information conditions, and action support that resolve hidden-confounding ambiguity for that particular contrast. Where those conditions fail or remain unverified, the effect is not established merely by proxy correlations. Whether LatentBridge also reaches matched return with ≥30% fewer environment interactions than recurrent PPO, counting probes, remains an open empirical question.

I want to state the LatentBridge hypothesis: under proxy exclusion, completeness, and overlap, it identifies unprobed action contrasts and saves at least 30% of environment interactions versus recurrent PPO. Is that precise enough to be testable?

It states the two claims and the conditions attached to identification, but each term needs a precise definition before it can be proved or tested. The causal claim is that LatentBridge identifies specified unprobed counterfactual action contrasts when proxy exclusion, completeness, and overlap hold. The separate performance prediction is ≥30% fewer environment interactions than recurrent PPO to reach matched return. The assumptions do not themselves establish the performance prediction.
What exactly is an unprobed contrast in this hypothesis?

It is a comparison of expected subsequent return under one action versus a specified alternative at an observed history, where that particular comparison has no direct randomized-probe support. ‘Unprobed’ does not mean the contrast is undefined or that neither action ever occurs observationally. The hypothesis proposes that valid negative-control proxies, subject to its three conditions, can identify such a contrast despite hidden confounding.
Does identifying it mean learning what would have happened under both actions on an individual trajectory?

No. The intended target is a defined counterfactual contrast in expected return. An individual trajectory reveals only the continuation following the action actually taken. Identifying an expected contrast does not disclose both potential outcomes for that individual decision.
How should the delayed return enter the definition?

Both alternative-action cases must use the same definition of subsequent return, including any delayed rewards relevant to the comparison, and a specified rule for later decisions. Otherwise a purported contrast might compare different outcomes or different continuations. The hypothesis does not specify a return horizon or a continuation rule, so those still need to be made explicit.
What does proxy exclusion mean without naming a particular proxy?

Conceptually, exclusion restricts which direct causal relationships an observed negative-control proxy may have with the action intervention or the return in the proposed identification argument. A proxy may be associated with return through hidden circumstances without being allowed an effect that violates its assigned negative-control role. The exact excluded relationship depends on how the proxy is defined; this hypothesis does not name one, so we should not claim a specific exclusion restriction has already been verified.
Would a proxy fail exclusion just because it predicts a delayed reward?

Not necessarily. Predictive association is different from the prohibited causal pathway specified by an exclusion restriction. A useful proxy may be associated with hidden circumstances that also affect return. Whether it meets exclusion requires the appropriate causal restriction, not merely a test of whether its correlation with reward is zero.
And what is completeness doing?

Completeness is the information condition: the proxies must distinguish relevant hidden influences sufficiently for the proposed observable relationships to pin down the action contrast, rather than leaving different causal explanations observationally indistinguishable. Its formal statement depends on the proxy roles and identification equations. The hypothesis invokes completeness; it does not provide a proof that any particular proxy set satisfies it.
So completeness does not mean we reconstruct the exact hidden state?

Correct. It concerns whether the available proxy information is sufficient for the specified causal inference, not whether every hidden circumstance becomes observable or can be labeled on each trajectory. A method could identify an expected contrast under appropriate completeness conditions without recovering an individual hidden state.
What role does overlap have if proxies address hidden confounding?

Overlap concerns support for the action alternatives in the comparison. Proxies cannot automatically tell us the return under an alternative action for which the relevant information has no support. Exclusion constrains causal relationships, completeness addresses information about hidden influences, and overlap addresses whether the compared actions are represented sufficiently for the intended identification argument.
Is observational overlap the same as randomized probing?

No. Both alternatives can occur in observational data without having been randomized. Overlap permits an observational comparison, but hidden circumstances may still influence which action occurs. The proxy exclusion and completeness assumptions are doing essential work in the hypothesis about those unprobed contrasts; overlap alone does not turn association into a causal effect.
If both actions occur after the same observed history, are all three conditions automatically satisfied?

No. Their occurrence may speak to overlap, depending on precisely how the target history and support are defined. It says nothing by itself about a proxy’s exclusion restriction or whether the proxies meet completeness. Nor does a shared recorded history guarantee that hidden factors influencing choice and return have been accounted for.
Could there be overlap but incomplete proxies?

Yes. Observing both actions does not ensure the proxies contain enough information to resolve hidden-confounding ambiguity. Two causal accounts could agree on the observed histories, actions, proxies, and delayed returns yet imply different effects of intervening on an action. Unless the conditions rule out that ambiguity, identification has not been established.
Could exclusion and completeness hold but overlap fail?

That possibility also illustrates why the conditions are separate. Valid and informative proxies do not automatically supply support for an action alternative absent from the relevant comparison. Any claim to identify its contrast in that situation would require additional, explicitly justified restrictions not supplied by this hypothesis.
Does the hypothesis say LatentBridge identifies unprobed contrasts for every observed history?

No unconditional across-history claim follows. Identification is conditional on exclusion, completeness, and overlap for the target and information setting. A contrast at one history may have the necessary support and proxy information while another does not. The formal claim needs to specify its scope rather than treat ‘unprobed contrasts’ as every possible action-history pair.
What if an action is correlated with a delayed reward but intervention on it has no effect?

Its relevant counterfactual return contrast is zero even if it predicts reward in observed trajectories. Under valid identification conditions, the aim is to distinguish that contrast from an observed association distorted by hidden factors. The hypothesis does not claim that every correlated distractor has already been recognized or that a finite estimate must equal zero exactly.
Would randomized probes still matter if the proxy conditions identify an unprobed contrast?

Yes, but their evidential role is different. A valid randomized probe can support the action comparison it actually covers, whereas the claimed identification of an unprobed contrast relies on exclusion, completeness, and overlap. The hypothesis does not give a rule for combining probe and proxy evidence or say that a probe is required for every contrast called ‘unprobed.’
Could a probe at a different history verify proxy exclusion everywhere?

No. An intervention-based contrast at one history does not by itself prove that a proposed proxy satisfies its causal restrictions for all other histories. It can provide a useful comparison where it applies, but the identification assumptions for an unprobed target need their own justification.
Would identifying a proximal contrast prove that LatentBridge’s uncertainty-gated advantages improve learning?

No. Identification establishes what can be inferred about the specified action intervention under the assumptions. Using estimates as gated advantages to train recurrent PPO is a further step, and its environment-interaction efficiency must be evaluated separately. The ≥30% saving is a prediction, not a mathematical consequence of proxy exclusion, completeness, and overlap.
What exactly is the denominator of ‘at least 30% fewer interactions’?

Recurrent PPO’s environment-interaction count to reach the matched return is the reference. LatentBridge would need no more than 70% of that count for the comparison being reported. The percentage does not mean a 30% increase in return or a reduction of 30 interactions.
Do the randomized probes count toward LatentBridge’s interaction total?

Yes. Probe actions taken in the environment are environment interactions, even if they help estimate contrasts. An efficiency comparison that used their information but omitted their interaction cost would not test the stated savings prediction fairly.
Could LatentBridge count as saving 30% if it reaches a lower return with fewer interactions?

Not for an interactions-to-matched-return comparison. Both LatentBridge and recurrent PPO must be assessed at the same specified return level. The hypothesis does not name a numerical return threshold, so an evaluation would need to state that level clearly.
Does this hypothesis specify a task set, seed count, proxy variables, or probe budget?

No. It specifies proxy exclusion, completeness, and overlap as conditions for the unprobed-contrast claim, and ≥30% interaction savings versus recurrent PPO as the performance prediction. It does not name tasks, runs, proxies, an estimator, or a probe fraction. Those details cannot be supplied as though they were already part of the hypothesis.
Could favorable interaction savings be taken as evidence that exclusion and completeness hold?

Not on their own. A policy can learn efficiently using signals that predict return without those signals identifying causal action effects. The assumptions supporting unprobed contrasts require their own argument or assessment. Conversely, a sound identification argument would not tell us how many environment interactions recurrent PPO training needs.
